video_title: Why Defense, Not Offense, Makes You a Profitable Trader · Tim Furey
gist: Tim Furey, CEO of retail broker Trade View Markets and former Chicago Board of Trade market maker, argues profitable trading comes from defense (strict loss limits, only trades with a clean exit) and trend following, and shares brokerage-business and near-death anecdotes.

insights.claim: The clearing firm training floor market makers at the Chicago Board of Trade taught only loss control: a trader could lose at most about five ticks on a trade, anything over 10 ticks required an explanation, and 15 ticks meant suspension.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Hard, enforced loss limits were the training mechanism that produced profitable floor traders.
insights.quote: you had to learn how to lose

insights.claim: Furey made $28,500 in one month as a late-1990s Dow market maker, and when he asked the managers how to make money they told him profit comes from not losing it; he took away that there are no tricks beyond defense.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Consistent small losses with few outsized ones, not clever entries, drove his month.
insights.quote: That's how you make money is by not losing it

insights.claim: The 'power of the lean' means only entering trades where you can exit at break even: bid at 50, offer at 55 immediately, and if the market turns, get out at 50, so entries are chosen for exit certainty.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Pick trades by how cleanly you can exit rather than by how much you could make.
insights.quote: It's called the power to lean

insights.claim: Furey says the best trade can be not trading at all: walking away for a day or a week and waiting for the one setup where the gut says to put it on.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Inactivity is a position; it preserves capital for high-conviction setups.
insights.quote: that could be your best trade is not trading to walk away

insights.claim: A top Board of Trade bond trader reportedly earning about $100 million a year avoided CNBC, calling it a 50-minute infomercial with biased news, watched the sports channel on big report days, and traded reactively with no opinion on direction.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Elite traders may deliberately avoid narrative input to keep a clear, reactive mind.

insights.claim: Furey is a trend trader using relative strength and weakness, says he does not use Bollinger bands, and holds that the strong get stronger and the weak get weaker.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: His rule set favors buying strength over indicator-based mean reversion.
insights.quote: The strong gets stronger and the weak get weaker

insights.claim: Chart test from a veteran 1990s trader: print the chart, put it on the floor, stand on a chair and squint; if it is going up, do not short it.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: A simple visual trend filter keeps traders from fading obvious trends.

insights.claim: Furey argues one should never try to trade a bubble burst: in the 1990s Yahoo ran from $10 to about $400 while analysts called it a bubble and even professional pit traders were tempted to short it and were wrong for a long time.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Shorting on valuation alone ahead of the top is a common and costly error in strong trends.
insights.quote: You should never even try to go for a bubble burst in the market

insights.claim: Market structure heuristic: a healthy market goes up like an escalator and down like an elevator, so sharp sell-offs in an uptrend should be treated as places to buy.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Dips in strong trends are buy opportunities rather than reversal signals.

insights.claim: Across thousands of self-directed clients at his brokerage, Furey says the most common mistake is contrarian prediction: shorting because a market went up or buying because it went down.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Retail losses are linked to fading moves on the assumption of overvaluation; the opposite approach is trend-following.
insights.quote: They think high and it can't go higher. It guess what? It can.

insights.claim: Furey calls shorting gold last year his worst trade because it broke his trend-following rules; he shorted because it looked toppy while oil and other markets were behaving differently, and says nobody knew why gold was going to rise so much.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Even a rule-based trader gets hurt when he fades relative strength, which supports his rule-discipline claim.

insights.claim: Furey admits he holds a large, undefended long position in Tesla, with no profit target and no defense, which he calls the worst thing you could do in trading since he has an opinion on it, because he rates the technology and Elon Musk highly.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: The speaker contradicts his own defensive rules on this one name, so it is conviction and not a system signal; he explicitly says he could be wrong.

insights.claim: Furey says professional traders should not rely on trading income for a mortgage and family; his advice is to trade as a hobby or part-time because losing years are inevitable and a bad year with fixed obligations is ruinous.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Position sizing in life matters: personal financial leverage forces bad trading decisions.

insights.claim: A first outsized win can ruin a trader: Furey's parents forced him to sell LA Gear at about $14 from an $8 entry on $5,000, and he says the stock later reached $60 with splits, which would have been worth over a million, but he thinks an early windfall would have destroyed his drive.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Early big wins can undermine the hunger and discipline needed for durable trading.

themes.theme: Retail brokerage economics and business model

insights.claim: Furey likens a retail broker to the general-store owner in a gold rush: traders chase riches while the broker sells picks and shovels, and he says he gains a pulse on the market from onboarding about 300 new clients a day worldwide.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Venue and infrastructure providers capture steadier economics than the participants who trade.
insights.quote: the guy that owns the general store

insights.claim: Furey claims brokerage is far more scalable than a restaurant because it operates 24 hours with effectively unlimited seats and costs that barely rise as client accounts grow, and says he will only run scalable businesses.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Marginal-cost economics of digital brokerage underpin high operating leverage.

insights.claim: Furey says barriers to entry in retail brokerage have risen sharply: he self-funded Trade View around 2006-2007 with all his savings, but today he would need outside investors and a ton of capital, and cyber security has become a major new cost with expert staff on payroll.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Compliance, capital and cyber costs favor incumbents and scale in the brokerage industry.

insights.claim: Furey says a payment processor of his brokerage was hacked about eight or nine years ago and $3 million was taken, though it was caught early and recovered.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Illustrates operational and fraud risk for brokers beyond market risk.

insights.claim: Furey says he delayed entering Bitcoin because, running a brokerage with audited financials, he distrusted an asset with no audited financials and worried about hacking; he regrets missing the $300 and $3,000 levels and has since built his own crypto exchange, Yimmit.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: A regulated-broker mindset kept some traditional financial firms out of crypto early, and many now build their own exchanges after the fact.

insights.claim: Furey says client trading volume at his brokerage flows to whatever market is moving, with equities at highs and crypto the hot area drawing the most activity.
insights.speaker: Tim Furey
insights.so_what: Retail activity is momentum-chasing, which suggests broker volumes are pro-cyclical.
insights.quote: Whatever market is moving is where people gravitate to
